intro: Two harps glitter above the strings in Berlioz’s ballroom. The beloved’s melody joins the waltz, vanishes into the crowd, then returns for one last glimpse.

sections.label: Intro · Trembling strings and two harps
sections.mNote: Rising harp figures lead towards the dance

sections.label: A · The violins begin the waltz
sections.mNote: An A-major tune above plucked bass notes

sections.label: B · The beloved at the ball
sections.mNote: Flute and oboe give the idée fixe a dancing step

sections.label: A′ · The waltz returns in A
sections.mNote: Strings and winds take up the dance again

sections.label: B′ · A clarinet glimpses the beloved
sections.mNote: The strings fall silent for a short recollection

sections.label: Coda · The whole ballroom spins
sections.mNote: Tempo primo con fuoco: the dance rushes to its close

cues.title: Harps over trembling strings
cues.text: The strings tremble quietly while two harp parts enter in turn, climbing through broken chords. The sound swells towards the ballroom. Then the first violins begin the waltz.
cues.evidence: Movement II, bars 1–38, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 1–4: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violins begin to dance
cues.text: The waltz opens softly in A major. First violins carry the tune; cellos and double basses pluck the first beat of the bar. The melody rises and turns above that steady dancing step.
cues.evidence: Movement II, waltz from bar 38, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 4–5: violin melody and pizzicato bass accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The beloved in the crowd
cues.text: Berlioz’s programme puts the artist in the middle of a brilliant party. He sees his beloved there, just as he sees her in the countryside. The ballroom has its own music, but she brings the melody that has haunted him since the symphony began.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, programme of Symphonie fantastique, part II, in the 1845 and 1855 versions: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: The idée fixe waltzes
cues.text: Flute and oboe take the beloved’s melody, now reshaped into three beats to the bar. The strings keep the dance beneath it, with soft chords above running cello and bass figures. A clarinet joins the recollection.
cues.evidence: Movement II, bars 120–162; flute and oboe begin the idée fixe, followed by clarinet. Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 11–14.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A new ending in Florence
cues.text: In Florence in April 1831, Berlioz returns to the ballroom on paper. He reorchestrates the movement and writes a new coda, although the waltz has already pleased the audience at the Paris première.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 34, and the composition history at http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm : Florence, April 1831, reorchestration and new coda.

cues.title: The dance fills the room
cues.text: The waltz returns in A major. Its tune moves between strings and woodwinds, while the harps add rippling figures and bright chords. The private recollection has passed; the dancers are still turning.
cues.evidence: Movement II, returning waltz following the central idée fixe, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 15–23.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A clarinet remembers her
cues.text: The strings fall silent. A solo clarinet begins the idée fixe again, with a brief flute phrase, quiet horns and harp chords around it. The melody has only a few bars before the dance sweeps it away.
cues.evidence: Movement II, bars 302–319, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 31–32; the string parts rest through the exposed continuation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The ballroom catches fire
cues.text: Tempo primo con fuoco — the first tempo, with fire. The strings rush back, the woodwinds join them, and both harp parts throw in chords. A major carries the dance to its emphatic finish.
cues.evidence: Movement II, coda from bar 320, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 33–37: tempo marking, orchestration and A-major ending.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The violins step into the waltz
transitions.from: Intro · Trembling strings and two harps
transitions.to: A · The violins begin the waltz
transitions.how: The rising harps and trembling strings subside. First violins begin the waltz softly in A major, while cellos and basses pluck the first beat. Second violins and violas supply the lighter chords between those bass notes.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, bars 32–49; Michel Austin’s score transcription, p. 4.

transitions.title: The wind players recognise the beloved
transitions.from: A · The violins begin the waltz
transitions.to: B · The beloved at the ball
transitions.how: The A-major waltz dwindles to soft string chords. Flute and oboe begin the idée fixe in the same triple metre. Cellos and basses add running figures below it, and the clarinet takes up the melody as the phrase continues.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, bars 111–137; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 11–12.

transitions.title: The strings take the floor again
transitions.from: B · The beloved at the ball
transitions.to: A′ · The waltz returns in A
transitions.how: The wind melody finishes and the strings begin to rise. A major returns with the waltz: plucked bass notes hold the first beat, bowed strings carry the quick figures, and winds and horns answer above them. The triple metre stays in place.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, end of the central idée fixe and return, bars 156–192; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 14–17.

transitions.title: The strings leave the clarinet alone
transitions.from: A′ · The waltz returns in A
transitions.to: B′ · A clarinet glimpses the beloved
transitions.how: The waltz slows and the strings stop. A solo clarinet recalls the idée fixe while quiet horns and harp chords support it; the flute adds a short answer. The string bass has disappeared with the dancers’ regular tread.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, bars 298–319; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 31–32.

transitions.title: The strings rush back with fire
transitions.from: B′ · A clarinet glimpses the beloved
transitions.how: The clarinet’s recollection ends. At Tempo primo con fuoco, the strings return in A major with quick rising figures; the wind players and both harp parts join the rush. Bass notes and repeated chords drive the last bars home.
transitions.evidence: Movement II, bars 320–368; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 33–37.

source.title: Berlioz, Un bal — orchestral score without the optional cornet
source.locator: Introduction and waltz, bars 1–119; central idée fixe, bars 120–162; short return, bars 302–319; coda from bar 320.

timeline.note: Trembling strings prepare the successive entries of the two harp parts.
First violins carry the waltz over bowed inner strings and plucked bass notes.
Woodwinds and strings exchange the dance tune; harps add chords and rising figures.
Flute and oboe introduce the idée fixe above soft string chords; clarinet joins them.
The returning waltz spreads from strings to woodwinds, horns and harps.
A solo clarinet recalls the beloved, with brief flute, horn and harp phrases. The strings rest.
Strings, winds and both harp parts drive the final dance in A major.

composer.background:
When the young Hector Berlioz read aloud the death of Dido, his voice failed him. His father closed the book and announced that he was tired, allowing the boy to escape without having to explain his tears. Berlioz remembered the kindness in his Mémoires. Louis Berlioz was a doctor in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, and taught his son Latin, history and geography. He expected Hector to follow him into medicine. The boy learnt flute and guitar, pored over maps of distant islands and took Virgil’s abandoned queen personally.

In 1821 he went to Paris to study medicine. His first visit to the dissecting room at the Pitié hospital, he later wrote, ended with a flight through a window. On the second visit he managed perfectly well. Music was the more durable obstacle. He heard Salieri’s Les Danaïdes at the Opéra and began singing its airs over the cadavers. At the Conservatoire library he copied and memorised Gluck’s scores. His father argued, threatened and withheld support. Hector took composition lessons with Jean-François Le Sueur.
